newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: High liquidity, yen rise spark Seoul stock rally.
newsitem.headline: High liquidity, yen rise spark Seoul stock rally.

text.p: High cash liquidity and the yen's renewed strength against the dollar sparked a rally on the Seoul stock market on Monday which analysts said would likely continue through the month.
"This is basically driven by ample liquidity as reflected by falling interest rates," said Yi Seung-gook, head of research at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett Asia Ltd's Seoul branch.
"I see this rally lasting through the rest of the month before a correction sets in."
The South Korean composite stock index surged 1.6 percent, or 12.24 points, to 775.01 on Monday, the highest close since it reached 780.08 on October 28. Gainers led decliners 517 to 277.
Securities shares sparkled, with almost all rising by the daily limit of eight percent. The sector's sub-index was up 7.64 percent, or 104.85 points, at 1,476.52.
"Investors believed low interest rates would greatly help boost the earnings of securities firms because they heavily depend on borrowings," said Hyundai Securities analyst Koh Kyung-bae.
South Korea's benchmark three-year corporate bonds fell seven basis points to close at 11.38 percent, the lowest since June 11, 1996.
Bond market dealers said the source of the liquidity was a reluctance among financial institutions to extend fresh loans as a result of this year's string of corporate failures.
Since the recent collapse of several major firms, including Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, financial institutions have tightened credit.
The resulting high liquidity in the banking system is seen as causing the lower interest rates, which in turn are emboldening investors to buy shares.
The Bank of Korea on Monday sold one trillion won ($1.12 billion) worth of 364-day Monetary Stabilisation Bonds to absorb surplus cash from the banking system.
"Buying sentiment was strong today despite the central bank's effort to mop up liquidity," said Kang Yung-gee, a bond dealer with Hyundai Securities.
Monday's fresh rebound of the yen to its highest level against the dollar since last November also rekindled buying interest in the hope that an economic recovery was in sight.
The yen briefly rose to 111.80 per dollar at midday in Tokyo before retreating to around 112.90 yen.

A stronger yen would boost South Korean competitiveness for a wide range of items. South Korean manufacturers compete mainly with Japan in their key export markets and a stronger yen makes Japanese products more expensive overseas.
The yen's strength sparked buying in shares of Daewoo Heavy Industries Co, the largest listed South Korean shipbuilder. Daewoo closed up 330 won at 8,580 after touching a year high of 8,650.
But analysts said disappointing corporate results for the first half of the year were expected to emerge around the end of this month, which could cause a correction.
"We are hearing that most companies saw no improvement in their first-half performance," said Yi of ABN AMRO.
"Corporate earnings are now attracting little attention but more detailed news will flood in later this month and will begin affecting the market."

South Korean companies suffered a sharp deterioration in annual earnings last year due to a cyclical downturn in the economy coupled with a slump in exports caused by depreciation of the yen against the greenback.
(Conversion: $1 = 891 won)
